title: WISP 00: WISP process and document format
implementation: Process proposal
summary: Separate Ghost, the small rendezvous primitive, from Ghostly, its reference application, and make independently implementable extensions reviewable. WISP is the working document name; this draft does not decide its expanded acronym.

title: WISP 01: Ghost Core Protocol
implementation: Existing rendezvous and DHT text; the DHT as rendezvous and floor of every chat (decided 2026-09-25; being implemented)
summary: Ghost is layer 0 of every 1:1 chat (400). It is always the rendezvous: where the invite's keys meet, where the first contact and handshake happen (403), where each side publishes its presence, its capability record (03) and the signaling or descriptors a peer-to-peer transport needs (100). It is also the floor: when no peer-to-peer transport connects, or the one in use drops, short text and its receipts travel in bou

title: WISP 02: Peer Keys
implementation: Existing per-link keys; lifecycle extensions proposed
summary: The follow-up adds transcript-negotiated signed signaling, durable per-message delivery/retry state and observed extension interoperability; see the implementation profile for exact partial coverage and residual risks. This does not change Draft status.

title: WISP 03: Capability Negotiation
implementation: Existing advertisements and the paired pair-offer; the layer-0 capability record (decided 2026-09-25; being implemented)
summary: The one chat of 400 negotiates capabilities in two places:

title: WISP 04: Local Profiles
implementation: Experimental: web, desktop and browser extension clients
summary: A profile is a local container on one device. It holds everything a person may want to keep apart (for example "Personal" and "Work"), and exactly one profile is active in a running client. A profile is not a protocol identity: contacts never learn that profiles exist, how many there are, or their names. Each chat already has its own keys (02); a profile groups chats and everything tied to them.

title: WISP 05: Profile Backups
implementation: Experimental: web and desktop clients
summary: A profile backup captures one local profile (04) completely, so it can be brought back on this or another device: chats and their keys, messages and files, wallets and their payment journal, shared services and grants, per-chat payment choices and settings. It is one opaque, encrypted bundle. Where a bundle is kept (a file, an S3 bucket) is the concern of storage adapters (1000); this document defines what a bundle i

title: WISP 100: Transport Negotiation
implementation: Experimental rank-sum negotiation in every new chat; the DHT floor, background retry and upgrade (decided 2026-09-25; being implemented)
summary: Every 1:1 chat of 400 has two layers. Layer 0 is the DHT: the rendezvous, and the floor that carries short text (403) when nothing else connects. Layer 1 is the transport this document selects: WebRTC (101), Iroh (102) or HyperDHT (103).

title: WISP 1000: Storage Contract
implementation: Experimental: local file (1001) and S3-compatible (1002) adapters
summary: Storage keeps encrypted bundles (05) somewhere other than the running profile: a file the person holds, a bucket, later a WebDAV share or a relay. The 10xx family defines one contract that every place implements, so backups, and later continuity features, do not depend on any single provider. Storage never sees plaintext and never decides what a bundle contains.

title: WISP 1001: Local File Storage
implementation: Experimental: web and desktop clients
summary: The simplest place: a file the person keeps. It needs no account, network or credential.

title: WISP 1002: S3-Compatible Storage
implementation: Experimental: web and desktop clients; exercised against a local S3-compatible server
summary: Any service speaking the S3 object API: AWS S3, Cloudflare R2, Backblaze B2, Wasabi, MinIO, Garage and others.

title: WISP 101: WebRTC
implementation: Existing adapter behavior; WISP binding proposed
summary: WebRTC is one layer-1 candidate of the one chat (400, 100), and the only one in browsers and the extension. Its rtc signaling rides layer 0, in the link's own signed record, as today. A WebRTC attempt that does not connect (no ICE path, no TURN, a blocked network) no longer fails a first pairing: the chat stays on-dht and retries in the background. A WebRTC session that drops sends the chat to on-dht until it or anot

title: WISP 102: Iroh
implementation: Experimental native adapter of the chat session (desktop); relay-only browser build in the web app and the extension (2026-09-25); descriptors on the DHT (decided 2026-09-25; being implemented)
summary: Iroh is a native layer-1 candidate of the one chat (400, 100). Proposed: its endpoint id is published in the layer-0 capability record (03), so two desktops can try Iroh without a WebRTC session first (today its descriptor is exchanged only inside an authenticated session). The endpoint id is dialled through Iroh's own discovery; no address goes into the record. An Iroh attempt that fails leaves the chat on-dht, and

title: WISP 103: HyperDHT
implementation: Experimental native adapter of the chat session (desktop); browsers through a HyperDHT relay (web app, extension); descriptors on the DHT (decided 2026-09-25; being implemented)
summary: HyperDHT is a native layer-1 candidate of the one chat (400, 100). Its DHT is not the chat's layer 0: layer 0 is Pkarr on the Mainline DHT, and a HyperDHT lookup is part of dialling this transport. Proposed: its public key is published in the layer-0 capability record (03), so it can be tried without a WebRTC session first. A failed attempt leaves the chat on-dht; a dropped session sends it there until a transport is

title: WISP 200: Payment Negotiation
implementation: Existing payment frames; generic integration proposed
summary: Ghost negotiates payment methods and carries requests/results; it does not mandate a new wallet. Current pay-req, pay, pay-res frames use request/payment IDs, decimal-text amounts, an asset and ordered endpoints. Initial identifiers are cashu and btc-lightning-bolt11. Frames run only over the data link. The application currently includes Cashu wallet code; that is a reference integration, not a Core requirement.

title: WISP 201: Cashu
implementation: Existing application integration
summary: Ghostly currently uses Cashu tokens and mint-backed wallet operations. Requests advertise accepted mints; an in-band payment carries a token; the recipient attempts redemption and returns a result. The application keeps pending operations and recovery state. This functionality belongs to the application/payment component, not Core rendezvous.

title: WISP 202: Ark payments via Arkade
implementation: Experimental browser adapter, Arkade SDK 0.4.74; regtest evidence below. Every new profile starts with a Bitcoin mainnet wallet on arkade.computer.
summary: This adapter implements Ark payments using @arkade-os/sdk 0.4.74. Ark is the payment method; Arkade is the selected provider implementation. Bark is a second, separate Ark provider: not a separate currency, and not compatible with this one (a Bark wallet cannot pay an Arkade address). Arkade was selected because its TypeScript wallet, transaction preparation, operator/indexer clients and browser repositories fit the

title: WISP 203: Lightning
implementation: Existing invoice integration; Lightning sources (the Cashu mints by default)
summary: The current btc-lightning-bolt11 endpoint carries an invoice; the application supports Lightning through its Cashu component and invoice UI. This is not evidence of a universal external-wallet adapter or a locally operated Lightning node. BOLT 11 is the invoice format reference.

title: WISP 204: Ark payments via Bark
implementation: Experimental browser adapter, Second's Bark SDK @secondts/bark 0.24.0 (bark 0.7.1, WebAssembly). Testnet mode only: every Testnet profile starts a signet wallet on Second's server; Mainnet makes none yet. Regtest evidence below.
summary: Bark is Second's implementation of Ark: a client (bark) and a server (captaind). This adapter is a second Ark provider beside Arkade 202, and not interchangeable with it. Checked on 2026-09-23 against bark 0.7.1:

title: WISP 205: Lightning Addresses and LNURL-pay
implementation: Paying a Lightning address or LNURL through the active Lightning source; no wire format
summary: A Lightning address (name@domain, LUD-16) or an LNURL (lnurl1…, LUD-01; lnurlp://…, LUD-17) names an HTTPS service that hands out invoices on request (LUD-06). This draft covers paying one from a Ghostly client, in the wallet's Send tab and from an address pasted in a chat. Nothing crosses the data link: the chat carries the address as text, like any invoice. Receiving on a Lightning address needs a server the person

title: WISP 2xx: Fedimint ecash and Lightning through a federation
implementation: Experimental browser adapter on the Fedimint web SDK (@fedimint/core canary, pinned). Testnet mode only; regtest evidence below.
summary: Fedimint is a federation of guardians who hold bitcoin together (a threshold of them must agree on everything) and issue blinded ecash for it. It has three modules this adapter uses: mint (ecash notes), ln (Lightning through a gateway, a Lightning node that swaps ecash for HTLCs) and wallet (on-chain peg-in and peg-out, not used here yet). Joining a federation is trusting its guardians with the sats: custodial like a

title: WISP 2xx: Spark payments
implementation: Experimental browser adapter, Breez SDK Spark @breeztech/breez-sdk-spark 0.26.0 (WebAssembly, nodeless). Every Testnet profile opens a wallet on Breez and Lightspark's hosted regtest. Mainnet makes one only after the person enters a Breez API key.
summary: Spark is a Bitcoin layer 2. Its signing operators co-sign transfers of off-chain leaves: a transfer between two Spark wallets is instant, costs no on-chain fee, and needs no Lightning route. Before this draft Ghostly used Spark only through the Breez Lightning source (203, breez): it paid and received BOLT11 invoices from a Spark wallet. This adapter makes Spark a way of paying of its own, spark. Two contacts who bot

title: WISP 300: Identity Proofs
implementation: Identity proofs with a provider contract; Nostr first. See 2026-09-23
summary: External identity is an optional attestation about a participation, not the session's transport or its per-message signer. No external proof adapter was found in current core/browser code. A participant may offer multiple proofs or none; local/channel policy decides whether any are required.

title: WISP 301: Nostr
implementation: Nostr identity-proof provider; see 2026-09-23
summary: Optional Nostr proof of a Ghost participation. No implementation was found. NIP-01 defines Nostr's signed event structure; it does not define this Ghost proof or reserve a Ghost event kind.

title: WISP 3xx: Pubky
implementation: Experimental local import and modified-Ring adapter; see follow-up
summary: Optional Pubky identity proof bound to a participation. Existing Pkarr use and Paykit-inspired payment identifiers do not constitute Pubky identity integration. The browser documentation explicitly describes the current lack of Pubky Ring integration.
notices: Release decision (2026-09-21): external identity proofs and external profile lookup are deferred. This release exposes only Ghostly participation identity. Nostr, Pubky, Keet, imports and Ring UI are disabled; previous experiments and stored data are preserved for future work. Descriptions below are historical/research, not available release features.
Planned integration. No current integration is enabled or promised. The historical document identifier 302 remains in the URL for link compatibility; it is not a committed WISP number.

title: WISP 3xx: Keet
implementation: Blocked on existing-identity signer API; see follow-up
summary: Investigate an optional Keet identity proof. This is a feasibility draft, not a claim that Keet exposes an appropriate signing API, public identity format or bridge. Keet's official site describes the product; it is not evidence of a Ghost integration contract. No local adapter was found.
notices: Planned integration. No current integration is enabled or promised. The historical document identifier 303 remains in the URL for link compatibility; it is not a committed WISP number.

title: WISP 3xx: AT Protocol identity (Bluesky)
implementation: In development: packages/core/src/atprotoRepo.ts, atprotoIdentity.ts, packages/browser/src/proofs/atproto/, proofs/providers/atproto.ts; the client metadata goes live with the website
summary: A person shows one contact that they control an AT Protocol account (a Bluesky account, or one on any other Personal Data Server). The evidence is a record in the account's own repository, which the account's key signs; the contact checks it from the repository, without logging in anywhere and without a Ghostly server.

title: WISP 3xx: Bitcoin Address Proof
implementation: Experimental provider bitcoin (packages/browser/src/proofs/providers/bitcoin.ts); verifier in @ghostly/core
summary: An optional proof that the person can sign with the key behind a Bitcoin address. It follows WISP 300's two layers: the person signs, once, in their own wallet, the binding statement by which the address authorizes their Ghostly profile key for a validity window; per chat, the app presents that binding with a presentation signed by the profile key and bound to the chat, the contact and a fresh challenge, without aski

title: WISP 3xx: Profile DID (did:dht)
implementation: Experimental, web, desktop and extension: packages/core/src/didDht.ts, packages/browser/src/engine/did.ts, src/components/identities/PublicDid.tsx, Desktop publishsignedpacket
summary: Every Ghostly profile has a W3C Decentralized Identifier of the did:dht method (DIF, specification version 0): a DID document written as DNS records into the Pkarr packet of an Ed25519 key and stored in the Mainline DHT as a BEP44 mutable item, the same mechanism Ghostly uses for chats (01). Any did:dht resolver reads it, with no Ghostly server involved.

title: WISP 3xx: Decentralized identifiers (DIDs)
implementation: Experimental provider did; see below
summary: An optional identity proof, under 300, that a person controls a W3C decentralized identifier. The DID vouches, once, for the WISP 300 binding statement, which authorizes the profile's own proof key for a validity period; each chat the proof is shared with then gets a presentation signed by that proof key (shared WISP 300 machinery, no DID involved). A contact's app resolves the DID itself and checks the evidence agai

title: WISP 3xx: Domain Proofs
implementation: Experimental provider domain: packages/core/src/domainProofs.ts, packages/browser/src/proofs/domain.ts, packages/browser/src/proofs/providers/domain.ts
summary: A person shows a contact that they control a domain name, such as example.com, by publishing a record under it. It is an optional identity proof under 300 and the provider contract: chat works without it, it is shared with one contact at a time, and it says nothing about who holds the domain in law.

title: WISP 3xx: Nostr social layer
implementation: Experimental: packages/browser/src/nostr/, packages/browser/src/engine/nostrSocial.ts; see below
summary: What a proven Nostr identity (301 under 300) lets a person show and do in Ghostly, as separate capabilities, each permitted on its own, exactly as the roadmap's layer table separates them:

title: WISP 3xx: Provider-attested identity (OpenID Connect)
implementation: In development: packages/browser/src/proofs/oidc/; provider clients not yet registered (checklist)
summary: A person shows one contact that an account at a provider (Google, Microsoft, Apple, GitLab, Twitch) signed in for this conversation. The evidence is the provider's own signed ID token; the contact checks it against the provider's published keys. No Ghostly server takes part.

title: WISP 3xx: OpenPGP
implementation: Provider openpgp in the identity-proof registry; see Implementation
summary: An optional proof that a participant controls an OpenPGP key (RFC 9580, and the RFC 4880 v4 keys people already have). The participant signs a Ghostly statement with their own tooling (gpg --clearsign, or gpg --detach-sign --armor) and gives the result and their public key to their app. Ghostly never holds the secret key, so the same flow works when the key lives on a YubiKey or another OpenPGP card: gpg asks for the

title: WISP 3xx: SSH keys
implementation: Experimental providers ssh, ssh-github, ssh-gitlab; see below
summary: An optional identity proof, under 300, that a person controls an SSH key. The key signs, once, the WISP 300 binding statement, which authorizes the profile's own proof key for a validity period; each chat the proof is shared with then gets a presentation signed by that proof key (shared WISP 300 machinery, no SSH involved). A contact's app verifies both locally. Variants prove a GitHub or GitLab account instead of a

title: WISP 400: Chat Messaging
implementation: Existing 1:1 messages; DHT text after a live link drops. The single layered chat of revision 0.2 (decided 2026-09-25; being implemented)
summary: There is one kind of 1:1 chat and one invite format. Every chat has two layers:

title: WISP 401: Chat Session
implementation: The layer-1 session of every new chat (paired-chat/1): WebRTC, and native Iroh/HyperDHT where supported. First contact on the DHT and automatic upgrade (decided 2026-09-25; being implemented); calls (calls/1) and shared apps (services/1) on the live session.
summary: This is the layer-1 session of the one chat of 400. Formerly "paired chat", it is no longer a kind of chat the person picks: every new chat is a paired-chat/1 chat, whose layer 0 is the DHT (403) and whose layer 1 is this session, when a transport connects. The wire identifiers (paired-chat/1, chat/1, the frame names) are unchanged.

title: WISP 402: Compatibility Chat (v0.4 Timestamp Profile)
implementation: Existing legacy 1:1 clients (v0.4 and earlier, the Rust CLI) and the read/write path kept in current apps
summary: Formerly "Legacy Timestamp Chat". This profile is not withdrawn: withdrawing it would cut off every contact still on Ghostly 0.4 and every chat made with it. It is retained for compatibility with a narrowed scope:

title: WISP 403: DHT Text
implementation: Existing envelope, limits and DHT-only mode (pair2d/ chats and paired fallback); as the floor and first contact of every chat (decided 2026-09-25; being implemented). Native DHT versus browser relays differ.
summary: This profile is the floor of every chat of 400: the delivery that works whenever both sides reach the DHT, whatever else fails. It carries:

title: WISP 4xx: Store-and-Forward for an Away Contact
implementation: Experimental: hold/1 in web, extension and desktop clients; exercised against a local S3-compatible server
summary: Today a message for a contact who is away reaches them only as short text through bounded DHT records (403); a picture or a payment request waits until both are online (401). This profile lets what is sent meanwhile be held (text, a small file, a payment request) and delivered when the contact is back, with bounds that are stated rather than implied. Nothing here replaces the paired session or the DHT text path; a ch

title: WISP 500: File Transfer
implementation: Existing 1:1 transfer
summary: In the one chat of 400, a file (a voice message included) travels over layer 1 with 501, or, while the chat is not live, in a hold (4xx, at most 8 MiB) when both sides allow it. It never travels in DHT records, split or whole: the floor of 403 carries text only. With neither available, the file waits in the sender's outbox with a cancel ("Sends when live") and goes when layer 1 is back (new; today attaching is refuse

title: WISP 501: Chat Files
implementation: Negotiated paired data links; WebRTC and supported native adapters.
summary: Formerly "Paired Files". This is how files travel in every chat of 400 while it is live. The wire (files/2, pf- frames) is unchanged. While the chat is on-dht or dht-chosen, files are held (4xx) or wait in the outbox for layer 1 (500); a transfer cut by a drop to the DHT fails as today and is retried whole when layer 1 is back, under its original ID.

title: WISP 502: Compatibility File Frames
implementation: Compatibility chats' live data links; both peers online.
summary: Formerly "Legacy File Frames". Retained, not withdrawn: a compatibility chat (402) with a contact on Ghostly 0.4 still sends and receives files this way over its legacy WebRTC link. A new chat uses 501 only. The number and file name stay.

title: WISP 600: Voice and Video
implementation: 1:1 calls and screen sharing in every chat: compatibility chats (call) and the chat session (calls/1, live only)
summary: This document defines common responsibilities and proposed extensions. Exact implemented encodings and runtime limits belong to 601 · WebRTC Media. Supporting a concrete profile does not establish full conformance to this Draft.

title: WISP 601: WebRTC Media
implementation: Compatibility chats (call) and the chat session of every new chat (calls/1); capture varies by platform.
summary: The implemented 1:1 profile uses compact call signaling and live call control frames, with ICE/fingerprint/candidate validation and a freshness window. Its v2 behavior pre-negotiates video so camera/screen changes can use replaceTrack; picture state is signaled separately. Call signal validation and the protocol define exact fields and legacy compatibility.

title: WISP 700: Local Services
implementation: Existing HTTP proxy, in every chat (desktop and extension hosts)
summary: This document defines common responsibilities and proposed extensions. Exact implemented encodings and runtime limits belong to 701 · HTTP Local Service Profile. Supporting a concrete profile does not establish full conformance to this Draft.

title: WISP 701: HTTP Local Service Profile
implementation: Desktop/extension hosting in every chat: data-link frames in compatibility chats, the same frames inside ph frames in the chat session (services/1); web viewer where supported.
summary: Control req frames carry request ID, service ID, method, path, sanitized headers and body presence. res carries status/headers/body presence; bounded binary chunks carry bodies and rst cancels/resets. Reject unknown/disabled/unauthorized service IDs, invalid methods/headers, target escape, excess body/concurrency and idle timeout. Do not inherit the host's cookies or local credentials.

title: WISP 800: Invite and Join
implementation: Existing bearer invite; admission protocol proposed
summary: Every new 1:1 chat starts from the same invite (801): one bech32m string, ghostly1…, also shareable as https://ghostly.tools/#ghostly1…. The invite no longer chooses how the chat is carried; the handshake does, on the DHT and on a stream in parallel (400). Its format version is the first data symbol, and the error rules go both ways: a current app answers a newer version with "Update to join", a failed checksum with

title: WISP 801: Implemented Invitation Profiles
implementation: Today: pair1/ and pair2d/ creation plus v0.4 imports. One bech32m format, ghostly1…, and the reading rules below (decided 2026-09-25; being implemented)
summary: A current app creates exactly one kind of invite, for the one chat of 400. There is no "Live chat" or "Text only" choice: how the chat is carried is decided after the handshake, and can be changed per chat at any time.

title: WISP 900: Group Session Negotiation
implementation: Two profiles: group-mesh/1 (private, up to eight) and group-community/1 (a link anyone can open, hundreds of members, admission by any member); core, engine, UI, e2e and a headless load test; text only
summary: Define how a group of Ghostly peers agrees on who is in it, protects what they say across membership changes, and moves it between them without touching Pkarr/DHT. Revision 0.1 was a proposal with every choice open. Revision 0.2 recorded the choices made for the first distribution profile, 9xx · Group Mesh. Revision 0.3 adds a second, 9xx · Group Community, for the group whose link is the way in: posted in a large co

title: WISP 9xx: GossipSub Transport
implementation: Proposed; no adapter found
summary: Evaluate GossipSub as an off-DHT distribution layer for group sessions. No Ghostly adapter was found. libp2p GossipSub v1.1 describes mesh/gossip routing and peer scoring; neither routing nor scoring is group encryption, membership consensus or guaranteed storage.
notices: Planned integration. No current integration is enabled or promised. The historical document identifier 901 remains in the URL for link compatibility; it is not a committed WISP number.

title: WISP 9xx: Group Community Distribution Profile
implementation: group-community/1: core protocol in groupCommunity.ts and communityRendezvous.ts; engine in community.ts, payments in communityPay.ts; UI shared with the mesh; unit tests, a six-browser e2e, a three-browser payments e2e and a headless load test
summary: A group whose link is the way in: posted in a large community, anyone who opens it joins, whether or not the admin is online, and the group holds hundreds of members, not eight. group-mesh/1 stays what it is (a small private group of contacts); a group says which of the two it is from its first commit, and never changes.

title: WISP 9xx: Group Mesh Distribution Profile
implementation: group-mesh/1: core protocol in packages/core and, for the group's link (group-entry/1), groupEntry.ts; engine, UI and four-browser e2e in packages/browser and e2e/web/groups.spec.ts; web, extension and desktop share it
summary: Payments between two members are part of it (§ Payments): the money travels on their edge, the group sees a note. Files, media, calls and local services are not part of this profile and are refused in groups.
